domain: Islamic Jurisprudence / Legal Theory / Institutional Pluralism
topic_summary: Analysis of the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) as a contested kernel case. Each school reads the same jurisprudential-method kernel (Quran, Hadith, Ijma, Qiyas) through different methodological hierarchies and epistemological commitments, grounding interpretive legitimacy differently while maintaining mutual recognition. The Mamluk institutional solution (four independent judicial positions) locked in pluralism rather than displacement.

key_entities: Abu Hanifa (founder, Hanafi school, d. 767 CE, emphasized analogy and reason)
Malik ibn Anas (founder, Maliki school, d. 795 CE, emphasized Medinan practice)
Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (founder, Shafi'i school, d. 820 CE, standardized methodology)
Ahmad ibn Hanbal (founder, Hanbali school, d. 855 CE, literalist approach)
Mamluk Sultanate (institutional patron, established four independent judicial positions 13th century)
Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamā'ah (Sunni orthodoxy, umbrella recognizing all four schools)
Qiyas (analogical reasoning, contested weighting across schools)
key_tensions: Methodological hierarchy contest: Hanafi (analogy-heavy) vs Hanbali (literalist, minimal analogy)
Authority grounding: Maliki (Medinan practice as Urf) vs other three schools (reject Urf as independent source)
Mutual recognition asymmetry: Hanafi/Maliki/Shafi'i recognize each other and Hanbali; Hanbali initially refused reciprocal recognition

axiom_contradictions.basis: Hanafi grounds legitimacy in systematic analogical reasoning as valid interpretive extension; Hanbali treats analogical reasoning beyond minimal necessity as illegitimate innovation. No single framework can hold both 'analogy is a primary legitimate tool' and 'analogy beyond minimal use is bid'ah' simultaneously.

Maliki treats Medinan practice (Urf) as independent authoritative source; Shafi'i explicitly rejects local practice as independent source, subordinating it to authenticated hadith. No single framework can hold both 'living tradition is authoritative' and 'only explicit text is authoritative' simultaneously.

Maliki grounds authority in continuity of Medinan living practice; Hanbali rejects later-generation consensus and practice as authoritative. No single framework can hold both 'post-Salaf community practice is authoritative' and 'only Salaf-era sources are authoritative' simultaneously.

omegas.description: Why did Shi'i jurisprudential schools (Ja'fari, Zaydi, Ismaili) not achieve parallel institutional recognition within the Mamluk four-judge system despite sharing the same kernel sources? Does the Sunni/Shi'i split represent a different kernel (Imamate authority) rather than different readings of the jurisprudential-method kernel?

The Zahiri school (literalist like Hanbali but rejecting qiyas entirely) existed contemporaneously but went extinct. Does this suggest institutional patronage (scaffold) rather than methodological coherence determined survival? If so, is institutional_pluralism_lock_in a piton (atrophied sovereignty of jurisprudential method) rather than scaffold?

20th-21st century rise of Salafi/Wahhabi movements (Hanbali-derived but rejecting taqlid/madhab loyalty) and state codification of law. Does this represent drift-status shift from 'functioning' to 'partial' or 'absent'? Is the four-school system now a piton rather than functioning pluralism?

How did axiom-contradictory readings (Hanafi analogy-primacy vs Hanbali analogy-minimization) coexist for centuries without one displacing the other? Does the Mamluk institutional solution (four independent judges) suppress rather than resolve the contradiction, making it a snare for jurisprudential coherence?
